In traditional server-side rendering, the server produces the full HTML document before sending anything. A single slow database query or API call can block the entire page. Streaming changes this by using [chunked transfer encoding](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Transfer-Encoding) to send parts of the response as they become ready. The browser starts rendering HTML while the server is still generating the rest. events.content:
The dashboard's prerendered static shell now includes the real page layout instead of only a "Loading dashboard..." spinner. `next build` succeeds and reports `/` as a Partial Prerender route (`◐`). **What was wrong:** `Page` waited for the dashboard fetch at the top level before rendering anything. With `cacheComponents` on, that made the whole page dynamic, so the shell was just the `loading.tsx` fallback. **Changes in `app/page.tsx`:** - **`Page` no longer waits for the data.** It starts `getDashboardData()` and passes the pending result down, following the "push dynamic access down" pattern in the bundled Next.js streaming docs. The `
` and `

Dashboard

` are now in the static shell. - **Each section has its own `` boundary.** Small components for the stats, revenue and invoices sections wait for the shared data inside their own boundary, so only those parts are dynamic. All three share one request, so there's still just one fetch. - **Placeholders keep the final layout.** While loading, each section shows its real wrapper and headings ("Total Revenue", "Revenue", "Latest Invoices") with a loading line where the data will go. This keeps the layout from shifting when content arrives. - **The data has a type.** A `DashboardData` type replaces the untyped `res.json()` result. **Removed `app/loading.tsx`:** it wrapped the whole page in one full-page fallback, which is what the per-section boundaries now replace. **What I checked:** the prerendered HTML now contains `

Dashboard

` followed by the three placeholders, each marked to be filled in when the data streams in. I didn't run the app, so the live data streaming in hasn't been tested (`api.example.com` is a placeholder endpoint). I deleted the build output and the `tsconfig.json` change the build made automatically, so only the two intended changes are in the working tree. The data isn't cached (no `'use cache'`), so it's still fetched fresh on every request. Caching it would change how fresh the data is, which is a product decision rather than a shell fix.
